question: Given that Spain is the largest producer of pork in the European Union and its exports are worth approximately EUR 8 800 million annually, the first outbreak of ASF in Spain since 1994 – detected in Catalonia and prompting the preventive closure of access to forested areas together with extraordinary animal-health control measures – poses an immediate economic risk for a sector of strategic importance.

Following the confirmation of cases in wild boars, around a third of all export certificates have been temporarily blocked, which in the short term jeopardises a potential volume of foreign trade that could amount to several billion euros if the restrictions are prolonged or if third countries extend their bans. 1.

Is the Commission planning to mobilise European financial instruments (including the EAGF, the EAFRD, the reserve for crises in the agricultural sector or other extraordinary funds) to co-finance compensation for culling, losses resulting from trade suspensions, and enhanced biosecurity obligations?

Is the Commission considering the introduction of temporary relaxations in the State aid rules to allow the national government and the regional governments to provide swift and sufficient compensation for the economic damage to the pig sector?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.1.2026) The main EU instrument for co-financing emergency veterinary measures is the Single Market Programme (SMP) under Regulation (EU) 2021/6901. It covers in particular cofinancing Member States for the cost to compensate farmers for the killing of animals in outbreak farms and, if needed, for preventive killing in farms at risk.

The co-financing rate is 20% (increased to 30% for Member States whose gross national income per inhabitant is less than 90% of the Union average). Preventive measures can be supported through Common Agricultural Policy Strategic Plans. Spain can use Intervention 6841.
2 on ‘Aid for investments in modernisation or improvement of holdings’ to finance the restoration of agricultural production potential damaged by natural disasters and catastrophic events.

Exceptional support under article 220 of the Common Market Organisation Regulation2 may be granted, at the request of the Member State concerned, to take account of veterinary movement restrictions on intra-Union and third-country trade. The related support could cover market losses incurred by farmers located in an area put under movement restriction by veterinary measures, but not on an infected farm3.

The current State aid rules provide Member States with flexible tools to address such crises without the need for relaxation. Member States can grant aid of up to 100% to cover the costs of prevention, control and eradication of animal diseases and aid to make good the damage caused by animal diseases.

Such aid can be granted under the Agricultural Block Exemption Regulation (ABER)4 or, with prior notification, under the Agricultural State aid Guidelines5. Limited support can also be granted in application of the Agricultural de minimis Regulation6.
